clue.text: Did they tear a strip off offenders ?

definitions.text: Did they tear a strip off offenders ?

parts.words: Did they tear a strip off offenders ?
parts.note: to tear a strip off someone is to scold them, but the clue also pictures people who strip away skin; the old nickname for Sir Robert Peel's policemen fits both

explanation.surface: A question about whether someone gave wrongdoers a dressing-down.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Peel founded the London police in 1829, and his officers were nicknamed after him; they dealt with offenders, and the word also describes people who strip off peel.
explanation.definitionFit: Early British policemen took a nickname from Sir Robert Peel, and the word also means those who strip skins away.

clue.text: Bacon's end hangs by the neck

definitions.meaning: bacon comes from a pig, and its curly rear appendage is the pig's end
a plait of hair hanging down the back of the neck

explanation.surface: Grim news that Bacon met his end on the gallows.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads Bacon as Francis Bacon and 'hangs' as an execution, but the first half is the pig's curly rear and the second a plait hanging at the nape.
explanation.definitionFit: A pig's curly rear appendage, and a braid of hair worn hanging behind the head.

parts.note: an academic post is called a chair, and a cushy one would be a soft, comfortable armchair

explanation.surface: A suggestion that academics have an easy life.
explanation.walkthrough: Professors hold 'chairs', so a cushy one would be an easy chair, which is also a padded armchair.
explanation.definitionFit: A padded armchair, and also what a soft professorship would be called since a university post is a chair.

clue.text: Llewellyn's better half returned to Surrey

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the chosen letters are read in the opposite direction
a better half is usually a wife, but here it means the larger half: five of the name's nine letters, taken from the front

explanation.surface: Llewellyn's wife went back home to Surrey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'better half' takes LLEWE, the larger five-letter front half of LLEWELLYN, and 'returned' turns it round to EWELL. Ewell is a town in Surrey, the county south-west of London, so the definition names the place by its county.
explanation.definitionFit: The town lies in the county of Surrey, near Epsom, so it is a place in that county.

definitions.meaning: sweet bread that has gone off would be soured bread, the fermented starter-based loaf
in North American slang a veteran prospector of the Klondike or Alaska, who carried a fermented starter

explanation.surface: An old man complaining that the sweetbreads taste off.
explanation.walkthrough: Sweetbread suggests offal, but read it as sweet bread that is off, which is sour. In Canada and Alaska the word also meant a veteran prospector, after the sourdough starter they carried.
explanation.definitionFit: Bread raised with a fermented starter, and a veteran prospector of the Yukon or Alaska.

clue.text: Not so much acid as Asian

definitions.text: Not so much acid as Asian

parts.words: Not so much acid as Asian
parts.note: the acid found in wine lees has a longer name; drop one R from it and you have an adjective for the Tatar people of Asia

explanation.surface: A comparison saying something is less sour than oriental.
explanation.walkthrough: Tartaric acid is the acid from grape lees; 'Not so much' tells you to take a little away, and removing one R leaves the adjective for the Tatars, a Turkic people of Asia.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes the Tatars, a Turkic people of central Asia and Russia.

parts.note: Jonathan Swift wrote 'A Tale of a Tub', and the wind section of a band holds large brass instruments whose names start with that vessel

explanation.surface: A fast story carried along on the breeze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swift' reads as fast, but it is Jonathan Swift, author of 'A Tale of a Tub'; 'the wind' is the brass and woodwind section of an orchestra, home to these deep brass instruments.
explanation.definitionFit: These are deep-voiced brass instruments played in the wind section of a band or orchestra.

parts.note: ropy suggests bad beer, but read it as bound by rope: a pub bound to sell one brewery's beer

explanation.surface: A complaint about a pub serving poor-quality beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ropy' means poor, but here it means tied up. In Britain a tied house is a pub owned by or bound to a brewery and so obliged to sell its beers.
explanation.definitionFit: A British pub bound by contract or ownership to sell only one brewery's beers.

definitions.meaning: a dictator is someone in sole power over a country
a straight-edged measuring stick lets a pen draw a line without wandering

explanation.surface: A tyrant tolerates no departure from the party line.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all about a tyrant, but the second half is the straight edge used for drawing lines that cannot deviate.
explanation.definitionFit: A sovereign who governs, and a straight-edged measuring strip that keeps a drawn line true.

parts.note: a tropical fruit is named after the sweet sauce often poured on apple pie, so adding that sauce to it would be overdoing things

explanation.surface: A question whether a topping is unnecessary on an apple.
explanation.walkthrough: Custard is the usual British partner for apple pie, but the custard apple is a tropical fruit with sweet creamy flesh, so serving custard with it would be superfluous.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet sauce of milk and eggs, which also names the creamy-fleshed tropical fruit of the Annona tree.

parts.note: an old word for a tale of adventure to read, which is also the surname of the hero in P. C. Wren's Foreign Legion novel

explanation.surface: A dandy who comes from the Berkshire town of Reading.
explanation.walkthrough: Reading looks like the Berkshire town, but it means reading matter: a geste is a romance or tale of exploits, and Beau is the first half of the title of Wren's 1924 Foreign Legion novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an archaic term for a story of brave deeds, and it completes the title of Wren's famous novel.

clue.text: Overheads going up as there is a drop in liquidity

definitions.text: Overheads going up as there is a drop in liquidity

parts.words: Overheads going up as there is a drop in liquidity
parts.note: read as finance it is business costs rising when cash runs short; read literally it is covers held over heads opening as raindrops fall

explanation.surface: A business report: costs rise while the firm's cash reserves fall.
explanation.walkthrough: Overheads, going up, drop and liquidity all sound like accounting terms, but the picture is rain: shelters held overhead go up when drops of liquid start to fall.
explanation.definitionFit: Rain shades are carried over the head and are put up when drops of rain fall.

parts.note: a handle is slang for a title, so those who make handles are monarchs conferring knighthoods, done with a tap of the sword

explanation.surface: Industrial action by the workers who make door or tool handles.
explanation.walkthrough: Strikes suggests walk-outs by factory staff, but a handle is a title, and a knighthood is conferred with a light blow of the sword on the shoulder.
explanation.definitionFit: Such honours were originally the ceremonial tap of a sword given when a knighthood was bestowed.

clue.text: Docked mount a fraternal invader has

indicators.note: a docked tail is cut short, so the word for the mount loses its final letter

parts.note: a mount is a horse that is ridden

explanation.surface: A horse with a cropped tail is owned by an invading brother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Docked' cuts the last letter from HORSE to leave HORS, then A follows. Horsa and his brother Hengist led the Anglo-Saxon invasion of Britain in the fifth century.
explanation.definitionFit: This Jutish leader invaded Britain alongside his brother Hengist, by tradition around AD 449.

clue.text: Hot coal needed for this fish

indicators.note: the letters have to be worked into a new shape, as dough is kneaded, to supply what is wanted here

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Hot coals are required to cook this fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot' gives H, as on a tap, and 'needed' tells you to rework H and COAL into a new order, which gives a small river fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A small freshwater fish of the carp order with whisker-like barbels round its mouth.

clue.text: What you can get from viewing tragedy on colour TV causes alarm

definitions.text: What you can get from viewing tragedy on colour TV causes alarm

parts.words: What you can get from viewing tragedy on colour TV causes alarm
parts.note: colour TV offers tint, and a tragedy makes you weep, so you get tint plus tears; the phrase for that is an old outcry raised in pursuit of a felon

explanation.surface: A warning that watching sad drama on a colour set can be upsetting.
explanation.walkthrough: Colour TV gives you a hue, and a tragedy gives you a cry; the phrase they make is the old public outcry raised to chase a criminal, hence an alarm.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means a loud public outcry, originally raised by townsfolk to pursue a criminal.

parts.note: a divorced couple are no longer a couple, so the word for separated railway wagons fits them too

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark warns that the word is not the usual synonym: it pictures a couple who have been unhitched, as trucks are when the link between them is undone.
explanation.definitionFit: Railway wagons that have been disconnected are described this way, and a divorced pair are no longer joined.

parts.note: a check pattern is made of crossing lines, as on a tablecloth
a spouse is a mate, a husband or wife

explanation.surface: Someone boasting of winning over a wife in a cross-hatched dress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'my' is only there for the surface. The definition, 'Win', is the chess sense: the move that ends a game.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess this is the move that traps the opposing king and wins the game.

clue.text: Feline drinker from a foreign clime?

definitions.text: Feline drinker from a foreign clime?

parts.words: Feline drinker from a foreign clime?
parts.note: a cat laps its milk, so a lapper would be a feline drinker; the word for someone from the far north of Scandinavia starts with that lapping

explanation.surface: A question about a cat that drinks and comes from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: A cat laps up milk, so the 'feline drinker' starts with LAP; the whole word describes a native of Lapland, the Arctic region of Scandinavia and Finland.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the Arctic region spanning northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia.

clue.text: It's forged, but what luck if it turns up !

definitions.text: It's forged, but what luck if it turns up !

parts.words: It's forged, but what luck if it turns up !
parts.note: a blacksmith forges it, and it is lucky both if you find one and if it is hung with its open ends upward

explanation.surface: A forgery, yet a stroke of good fortune if it is ever found.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forged' suggests counterfeiting, but it means made at a smithy. 'Turns up' means both 'is found' and 'is hung with its points upward', which tradition says keeps the luck in.
explanation.definitionFit: Smiths shape these iron hoof guards at the forge, and they are traditional good-luck charms.

clue.text: Lord, Harry, what a big dog you are leading !

indicators.note: Harry is addressed as walking in front, so his short name comes first in the word

parts.note: Hal is the traditional pet name for Harry, as with Shakespeare's Prince Hal
a Great Dane is a very large breed of dog

explanation.surface: Someone exclaiming at a nobleman called Harry walking an enormous dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'what a' only links. Viscount Haldane was a British statesman, Lord Chancellor and Secretary for War, so 'Lord' defines him.
explanation.definitionFit: Viscount Haldane was a peer and Lord Chancellor, so the name is that of a British lord.

indicators.note: something arranged curiously is set out oddly, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: MP stands for a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A politician who is, oddly enough, an airhead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'curiously' reorders the letters of MP and YET. The surface mocks the politician, but the word you want just means containing nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something with nothing inside, and by extension a mind lacking thought.

clue.text: Self and winged spirit turn into birds

indicators.note: to turn round means to face the other way, so the letters of both pieces together run backwards

parts.note: a fay is a fairy, pictured with wings

explanation.surface: A self and a fairy are transformed into birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' reverses SELF followed by FAY, SELFFAY, to give the plural of a dialect name for the green woodpecker, from its laughing call.
explanation.definitionFit: This English dialect word is a name for the green woodpecker, a kind of bird.

parts.note: Dives is the rich man of Luke's parable, who was clothed in purple and fine cloth woven from flax

explanation.surface: Someone grumbling that it's easy for rich people.
explanation.walkthrough: Dives looks like 'plunges', but it is the Latin name given to the rich man in Luke 16, who 'was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day'.
explanation.definitionFit: The rich man of the parable wore fine flaxen cloth, so the cloth fits his luxurious way of life.

parts.note: in a hunting game 'getting warm' means drawing close to the hidden object, so it is approaching

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase suggests a rising temperature, but in a children's hiding game 'you're getting warm' means you are drawing close.
explanation.definitionFit: In a hiding game, being told you are warm means you are approaching the target.

clue.text: A plain fact that is graspable and to the point

definitions.text: A plain fact that is graspable and to the point

parts.words: A plain fact that is graspable and to the point
parts.note: the old pointed pole that soldiers gripped gives the simile 'as plain as' it, so it is plain, can be grasped and has a point

explanation.surface: A clear, easily understood and relevant fact.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain', 'graspable' and 'to the point' all sound like praise of a clear argument, but each describes the wooden shaft of an old infantry weapon, remembered in the simile 'as plain as a pikestaff'.
explanation.definitionFit: The shaft of a soldier's spear was gripped in the hand and tipped with a point, and appears in a simile for obviousness.

indicators.note: here hard is read as roughly or with difficulty, a hint that the name is to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A man named Pedro worked hard at his books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hard' tells you to rearrange PEDRO, giving a past tense meaning studied closely; one could also read the whole of 'studied hard' as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To pore over something is to read or examine it closely, so the past tense means examined.

clue.text: That which binds. Lift it, and it breaks

indicators.note: in a down clue, to lift a word is to raise it from the bottom, so its letters are read in reverse

parts.note: parts means separates or breaks apart

explanation.surface: A riddle about something that holds things together but snaps when raised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lift it' turns the answer upward in the down grid, and what you then read is PARTS, meaning 'breaks'; so 'Lift' reverses PARTS to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A band of leather or cloth used to fasten or hold things together.

parts.note: a primate is a monkey and a conundrum is a puzzle, so this is the botanical Latin name of the monkey puzzle tree

explanation.surface: An archbishop's never-ending riddle set in Latin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primate' suggests an archbishop, but it is a monkey; with 'conundrum' as puzzle you get the monkey puzzle, an evergreen conifer from Chile, and the clue asks for its Latin genus name.
explanation.definitionFit: The monkey puzzle tree is a Chilean conifer, and its scientific genus name is wanted here.

parts.note: an eminence is a hill or mount, and the poet lived at a house called after a Lake District village with Mount added

explanation.surface: Praise of William Wordsworth's distinction as a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eminence' suggests fame, but it means a mount: Wordsworth lived from 1813 until his death at Rydal Mount, a house near Ambleside in the Lake District of northwest England.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet's home was Rydal Mount, so the village name before 'Mount' completes the reference to his hill.

clue.text: Easy, Des, to show you've tried

indicators.note: the letters are put on show in a new arrangement, so the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Telling a man called Des to take it easy and prove he has made an attempt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'show' tells you to rearrange EASY and DES, which gives a past tense meaning attempted. 'you've' only makes the surface read naturally.
explanation.definitionFit: To assay or attempt something is to make an effort at it, so the past form means attempted.

parts.note: read as an order to throw things out, it also describes goods sent out of a country, whose Latin roots mean carried out of port

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation sounds like a bouncer's order, but read with 'Out' as 'ex' and harbours in mind it describes goods shipped abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods sold abroad are sent out of the country, the opposite of imports.
